column6: Exodus opens with Moses seeing a bush aflame yet unconsumed, a fire that draws him toward revelation; the Qur'anic Moses likewise sees a fire while traveling, but the scene's signal leads into a different account of his call.

God calls Moses from within the burning bush after he approaches it; this makes nearness to fire the threshold of a divine summons, unlike the condemned person's inescapable entry into the great fire.
A pillar of fire leads Israel by night; it supplies the concrete scriptural counterpart to the commentary's distant fire as a route-finding sign, while its fire guides rather than consumes.
Joshua is called a brand snatched from fire amid Satan's accusation; the image sharply contrasts the commentary's person fixed in fire with one taken out of it by divine rebuke.

Isaiah shows the corpses of rebels where worm and fire do not cease; the next Qur'anic verse says the entrant neither dies nor lives, and Isaiah's corpses make the difference between the images worth keeping visible.

column5: Worm does not die; fire is not quenched
column6: Jesus cites the undying worm and unquenched fire for Gehenna; alongside the Qur'anic entrant who neither dies nor lives, this gives an explicit neighboring-scripture formulation of punishment beyond ordinary death.
The day burns arrogant evildoers like stubble and leaves neither root nor branch; this joins the commentary's great fire to pride and final judgment, not simply to a larger physical flame.

column5: Who can dwell with devouring fire?
column6: Isaiah's sinners ask who can live with devouring fire and everlasting burnings; the question directly frames the commentary's defining issue of what kind of person can abide in fire.

The following verse answers Isaiah's question with the one who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, then promises secure dwelling; it contrasts the Qur'anic wicked person's entry with an upright person able to dwell near divine fire.
John's winnowing separates wheat into the barn and burns chaff with unquenchable fire; it makes the commentary's two groups after admonition concrete as a sorting whose result is different fates.

column5: Eternal fire assigned to the condemned
column6: The king sends the cursed to eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels; fire is the assigned end of a class identified in judgment, matching the commentary's person defined by his destination.
Jesus pairs eternal punishment with eternal life as the two outcomes of judgment; this sharpens the Qur'anic contrast between the fire-bound person and the other person who prospers and prays.

column5: A dead rich man suffers in flame
column6: In the parable the rich man is dead yet conscious, tormented in flame and begging for water; it gives a specific image for enduring fiery suffering, while the Qur'anic following verse describes the state as neither death nor life.

column5: No crossing out of the place of torment
column6: Abraham says a fixed chasm prevents passage between the places of comfort and torment; this supplies a concrete account of the fire-bound person's inability to leave, like the commentary's gloss that yaslâ entails remaining with the fire.

column5: Sodom as an example of eternal fire
column6: Jude recalls Sodom and neighboring cities undergoing punishment of eternal fire; the shared judgment-by-fire story adds a scriptural precedent while the Qur'anic verse applies the fate to an unnamed individual.

An angel warns that anyone worshipping the beast and receiving its mark will drink God's wrath in fire and sulfur; the commentary's fire-as-identifying brand thus meets a text where allegiance-mark and fiery fate are explicitly joined.

column5: Smoke rises and the condemned have no rest
column6: The smoke of torment rises forever and the worshippers of the beast have no rest day or night; this makes the commentary's abiding in fire a specific unending condition.

column5: The lake of fire is called the second death
column6: Revelation names the lake of fire the second death, whereas the Qur'anic next verse says its entrant neither dies nor lives; the difference is a direct theological contrast in how fiery punishment is described.
Moses' song says divine anger kindles a fire that burns to Sheol below and consumes the land; its downward and encompassing reach gives a concrete cosmic scale to the commentary's great fire.
Moses calls Israel's God a consuming fire and a jealous God; this locates fire also in divine presence and judgment, not only in the condemned person's destination.

Hebrew צְלִי־אֵשׁ (roasted by fire), likely cognate with the source commentary's Arabic ص ل ي label, names Passover meat eaten at the meal; it preserves the cooking sense of the source's fire-verb family apart from punishment.
The proverb asks whether one can carry fire in the bosom without burning clothes; it gives a concrete counterpoint to controlled warming, showing that close contact with fire carries consequences.

column5: Walking on coals burns the feet
column6: The proverb asks whether one can walk on hot coals without scorching the feet; it makes bodily exposure to fire the issue, rather than merely seeing or approaching a distant flame.

The priestly law commands that fire remain continually lit on the altar; this is a persistent sacred fire maintained in worship, distinct from the punitive fire in which the commentary's person remains.

column5: Refiner's fire tests who can stand
column6: The messenger's coming is compared to a refiner's fire, with the question who can endure the day; it connects fire's severity to a test of the person rather than only to destruction.
The refiner sits to purify silver and the sons of Levi so they may offer rightly; this gives the commentary's metalworking fire a scriptural use that corrects and restores rather than merely burns.

column5: A fourth figure walks in the furnace
column6: Nebuchadnezzar sees four men walking unbound in the furnace, with a divine-looking fourth; fire becomes the setting of protected presence, contrary to the bound person's suffering in the great fire.

column5: The furnace does not burn the faithful
column6: Onlookers find that the men's bodies were unharmed and not a hair singed; this particular deliverance shows fire's force can be withheld, complementing the commentary's distinct fire of blessing and warmth.

column5: Passing through fire without being burned
column6: God promises Israel that when they walk through fire they will not be scorched; the image reverses the commentary's entrant who must bear the fire's full heat and cannot leave.

The Aramaic verse says Daniel kneels and prays three times daily; its צלי prayer verb is a cognate of the source commentary's prayer-form صَلَّى, while the commentary carefully distinguishes that prayer root from the fire-verb ص ل ي.

column5: Tested through fire and brought out
column6: The psalm says the people passed through fire and water before God brought them into abundance; fire names an ordeal one can survive, matching the commentary's secondary sense of suffering a hard trial.
Paul says the Day will disclose each person's work because fire tests what sort it is; like the commentary's fire that makes a person's identity legible, this fire exposes what the person has made.
Paul says a person's work may burn and he suffer loss, though he himself is saved as through fire; this provides a sharply contrary outcome to the one who remains inside punitive fire.

column5: Faith tested as gold by fire
column6: Peter compares tested faith to gold refined by fire; the metaphor supplies a specific trial-and-refinement sense for the commentary's claim that the fire-verb can name undergoing hardship.
Hebrews applies Moses' consuming-fire image to God; alongside the Qur'anic great fire, it keeps divine holiness and danger in view rather than treating fire only as a place.

column5: Sodom reduced to ashes as warning
column6: Peter says God reduced Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes and made them an example of what comes to the ungodly; this joins remembered fire judgment to present warning, as the commentary calls the fire itself an admonition.

Genesis Rabbah expands Abraham's story with Nimrod throwing him into a furnace and God rescuing him; the tradition makes fire a test that reveals fidelity and grants rescue, not simply an identity assigned by punishment.

column5: Gehenna's punishment has a stated limit
column6: The Talmud describes some sinners as judged in Gehenna for twelve months, after which bodies are consumed and souls burned; this later Jewish account contrasts with the Qur'anic description of a state in which the entrant neither dies nor lives.

column5: Abraham's and Balaam's disciples inherit different ends
column6: The Mishnah classifies disciples by their traits and assigns Abraham's disciples the world to come but Balaam's disciples Gehinnom; it gives a Jewish interpretive example of a person's defining way of life determining the destination.

column5: Furnace of Gehenna opposite a place of rest
column6: 4 Ezra reveals the furnace of Gehenna opposite a place of rest and delight; it concretely pairs fiery punishment with the other destiny, as the commentary's surrounding verses divide people into two outcomes.
